speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we approach the end of the year, it’s natural to look back on the progress that has been made toward our dual-mandate objectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased from its highs, and this has come without a significant increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s very good news.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But inflation is still too high, ongoing progress in bringing it down is not assured, and the path forward is uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we look ahead to next year, I want to assure the American people that we’re fully committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to achieve a sustained period of strong labor market conditions that benefit all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Since early last year, the FOMC has significantly tightened the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve raised our policy interest rate by 5¼ percentage points and have continued to reduce our securities holdings at a brisk pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our actions have moved our policy rate well into restrictive territory, meaning that tight policy is putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation, and the full effects of our tightening likely have not yet been felt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, we decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Given how far we have come, along with the uncertainties and risks that we face, the Committee is proceeding carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will make decisions about the extent of any additional policy firming and how long policy will remain restrictive based on the totality of the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that growth of economic activity has slowed substantially from the outsized pace seen in the third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Even so, GDP is on track to expand around 2½ percent for the year as a whole, bolstered by strong consumer demand as well as improving supply conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: After picking somewhat over the—up somewhat over the summer, activity in the housing sector has flattened out and remains well below the levels of a year ago, largely reflecting higher mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Higher interest rates also appear to be weighing on business fixed investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections (SEP), Committee participants revised up their assessments of GDP growth this year but expect growth to cool, with the median projection falling to 1.4 percent next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market remains tight, but supply and demand conditions continue to come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past three months, payroll job gains averaged 204,000 jobs per month, a strong pace that is nevertheless below that seen earlier in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains low at 3.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Strong job creation has been accompanied by an increase in the supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor force participation rate has moved up since last year, particularly for individuals aged 25 to 54 years, and immigration has returned to pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth appears to be easing, and job vacancies have declined.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed, labor demand still exceeds the supply of available workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: FOMC participants expect the rebalancing in the labor market to continue, easing upward pressures on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median unemployment rate projection in the SEP rises somewhat from 3.8 percent at the end of this year to 4.1 percent at the end of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased over the past year but remains above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Based on the consumer price index and other data, we estimate that total PCE prices rose 2.6 percent over the 12 months ending in November and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 3.1 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The lower inflation readings over the past several months are welcome, but we will need to see further evidence to build confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As is evident from the SEP, we anticipate that the process of getting inflation all the way to 2 percent will take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP is 2.8 percent this year, falls to 2.4 percent next year, and reaches 2 percent in 2026.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed’s monetary policy actions are guided by our mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship, as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are highly, highly attentive to the risks that high inflation poses to both sides of our mandate, and we are strongly committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I noted earlier, since early last year, we have raised our policy rate by 5¼ percentage points, and we have decreased our securities holdings by more than $1 trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our restrictive stance of monetary policy is putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee decided at today’s meeting to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent and to continue the process of significantly reducing our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While we believe that our policy rate is likely at or near its peak for this tightening cycle, the economy has surprised forecasters in many ways since the pandemic, and ongoing progress—sorry—ongoing progress toward our 2 percent inflation objective is not assured.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are prepared to tighten policy further if appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re committed to achieving a stance of monetary policy that is sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation sustainably down to 2 percent over time and to keeping policy restrictive until we’re confident that inflation is on a path to that objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While participants do not view it as likely to be appropriate to raise interest rates further, neither do they want to take the possibility off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy evolves as projected, the median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 4.6 percent at the end of 2024, 3.6 percent at the end of 2025, and 2.9 percent at the end of 2026, still above the median longer-term rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These projections are not a Committee decision or plan; if the economy does not evolve as projected, the path of policy will adjust as appropriate to foster our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In light of the uncertainties and risks, and how far we have come, the Committee is proceeding carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting, based on the totality of the incoming data and their implications for the outlook for economic activity and inflation, as well as the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In determining the extent of any additional policy firming that may be appropriate to return inflation to 2 percent over time, the Committee will take into account the cumulative tightening of monetary policy, the lags with which monetary policy affects economic activity and inflation, and economic and financial developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal and to keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to set the stage for achieving maximum employment and stable prices over the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—specifically on “any”: We do say that “in determining the extent of any additional policy firming that may be appropriate,” so “any additional policy firming”—that sentence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we added the word “any” as an acknowledgement that we believe that we are likely at or near the, the peak rate for this cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Participants didn’t write down additional hikes that we believe are likely, so that’s what we wrote down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But participants also didn’t want to take the possibility of further hikes off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s really what we were thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, of course, I don’t comment on, on any other officials, even those who work at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I’ll—but I’ll try to answer your question more broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the way—the way we’re looking at it is, is really this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When we started out, right, we said the first question is, how fast to move, and we moved very fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s really the question that we’re still on here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, we’re very focused on that, as I—as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People generally think that we’re at or near that and, and think it’s not likely that we will hike, although they don’t take that possibility off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—when you get to that question, and that’s your answer, there’s a natural—naturally, it begins to be the next question, which is when it will become appropriate to begin dialing back the amount of policy restraint that’s in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s really the next question, and that’s what people are thinking about and, and talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would just say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are seeing, you know, strong growth that is—that appears to be moderating; we’re seeing a labor market that is coming back into balance by so many measures; and we’re seeing inflation making real progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These are the things we’ve been wanting to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We still have a ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one is declaring victory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That would be premature.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we can’t be guaranteed of this progress [continuing].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re, we’re moving carefully in making that assessment of whether we need to do more or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s really the question that we’re on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, of course, the other question, the question of when will it become appropriate to begin dialing back the amount of policy restraint in place, that, that begins to come into view and is clearly a discussion—topic of discussion out in the world and also a discussion for us at our meeting today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it, it comes up in this way today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everybody wrote down an SEP forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So many people mentioned what their—what their rate forecast was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there was no back-and-forth, no attempt to sort of reach agreement like, “This is what I wrote down; this is what I think,” that kind of thing, and a preliminary kind of a discussion like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not everybody did that, but many people did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then, and I would say, there’s a general expectation that this will be—this will be a topic for us, looking ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That, that’s really what happened in today’s meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can’t do the head count for you in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s generally what happened today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think you can say that there’s little basis for thinking that the economy is in a recession now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think there’s, there’s always a probability that, that there will be a recession in the next year, and it’s a meaningful probability no matter what the economy is doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s always a real possibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The question is, is it—so it’s a possibility here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I have always felt, since the beginning, that there was a possibility, because of the unusual situation, that the economy could cool off in a way that enabled inflation to come down without the kind of large job losses that have often been associated with high inflation and tightening cycles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So far, that’s what we’re seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what many forecasters, on and off the Committee, are seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This result is not guaranteed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is—it is far too early to declare victory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there are certainly risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s certainly possible that, that the economy will behave in an unexpected way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has done that repeatedly through the post—in the post-pandemic period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, where we are is, is we see the things that I—that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think forecasters generally, if you go back a year, were very broadly forecasting a recession for this year, for 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And not only did that not happen—that includes Fed forecasters and really, essentially, all forecasters; a very high proportion of forecasters predicted very weak growth or a recession—not only did that not happen, we actually had a very strong year, and that was a combination of, of strong demand but also of real gains on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this was the year when labor force participation picked up, where immigration picked up, where the distortions to supply and demand from the pandemic—you know, the shortages and the bottlenecks—really began to unwind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we had significant supply-side gains with strong demand, and we got what looks like a 2½ percent-plus, or a little more than that, growth year at a time when potential growth this year might even have been higher than that, just because of the healing on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that was a surprise to just about everybody.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the inflation forecast is roughly, roughly what people wrote down a year ago, but in a very different setting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say the labor market, because of the stronger growth, has also been significantly better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look back at the SEP from a year ago, there was a significant increase in, in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It didn’t really happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re still at 3.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve seen, you know, strong growth, still a tight labor market but one that’s coming back into balance with the—with support from the supply side, a greater supply of labor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a—you know, that’s, that’s what we see, and I think that combination was, was not anticipated broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nothing quite that mechanical is happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think people are looking at what’s happening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think if you look at the big difference from September in the SEP, [it is that] the expectations for inflation this year, both headline and core, have come down, you know, really significantly in three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a big piece of, of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, [real GDP] growth has turned out to be very strong in the third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Now it] is slowing, we believe, as, as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve got—we’ve had several labor market reports, which suggest, again, significant progress toward greater balance across a very—a broad range of indicators.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re seeing so many of the indicators coming back to normal, not all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But so I think that people look at that, and they write down their—basically, each individual writes down a forecast and a rate forecast that goes with that forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We tabulate them and, and publish it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, that’s—that is—that is something that we’re very conscious of, and aware of, and monitor, and it’s certainly a big part of—it’s a part of how we think about things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, really, it’s broader financial conditions that matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as you well know, it’s so hard to know exactly, you know, what the—what the real rate is or exactly how tight policy is at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you couldn’t follow that like it was a rule and think that you would get the right answer all the time, but it’s certainly something that we’re focused on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, indeed, if you look at the projections, I think the expectation would be that the real rate is declining as we—as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, we—we’re—we don’t think about political events.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think about politics.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think about what’s the right thing to do for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The minute we start thinking about those things—you know, we just can’t do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll do the things that we think are right for the economy at the time we—when we think is the right time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’ll always do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I mentioned we’re moving carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One of the things we’re moving carefully about is that decision over—that assessment, really—over whether, whether we’ve done enough, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you see that people are not writing down rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s us thinking that we have done enough but not, not feeling that really strongly, confidently and not wanting to take the possibility of a rate hike off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, it’s not the base case anymore, obviously, as it was, you know, 60, 90 days ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s how we’re—that’s how we’re approaching things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, as I mentioned, we wrote down this SEP, and it talks about—people have individual assessments of when it will be appropriate to, you know, to start to dial back on, on the tight policy we have in place, and that’s a discussion we’ll be having going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s another assessment that we’re going to make very carefully, so as time goes forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this last year has been remarkable for the, the sort of seesaw thing, the back-and-forth we’ve had over the course of the year of markets moving away and moving back and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, and what I would just say is that we, we focus on what we have to do and how we need to use our tools to achieve our goals, and that’s what we really focus on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And people are going to have different forecasts about the economy, and they’re going to—those are going to show up in market conditions, or they won’t, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in any case, we have to do what we think is right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, in the long run, it’s important that financial conditions become aligned or are aligned with what we’re trying to accomplish, and, in the long run, they will be, of course, because we will do what it takes to get to our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, ultimately, that will mean that financial conditions will, will come along.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in the meantime, there can be back-and-forth, and, you know, I’m just focused on what’s the right thing for us to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And my colleagues are focused on that, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Listen, I welcome the progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s, it’s really good to see the progress that we’re making.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think if you look at the 12-month—look at the 6-month measures, you see very low numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at 12-month measures, you’re still well above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re actually above 3 percent on core, through November, PCE [inflation].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That isn’t to say—I’m not, you know, calling into question the progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just need to see more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We need to see, you know, continued further, further progress toward getting back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s what we need to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, our—it’s our job to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that—it’s one of our two jobs, along with maximum employment, and they’re equal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re very focused on, on, you know, doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, we’re moving carefully at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re pleased with the progress, but, but we see the need for further progress, and I think—I think it’s fair to say there is a lot of uncertainty about going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve seen the economy move in surprising directions, so we’re just going to need to see more further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll, we’ll look at the totality of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth is one thing, so is inflation, so is labor market data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’d, we’d look at the totality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we—as we make decisions about policy changes going forward, we’re going to be looking at all those things and, particularly, about the—as they affect the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s ultimately all about the outlook and the balance of risks as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what—that’s what we’d be looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we have stronger growth, you know, that’ll be good for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’ll be good for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It might actually mean that it takes a little longer to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will get it down to 2 percent, but, you know, if we see stronger growth, we’ll—we will set policy according to what we actually see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and so that’s how I would answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s only a problem inso—it’s not itself a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s only a problem insofar as it makes it more difficult for us to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, if you have—if you have growth that’s robust, what that will mean is probably it will keep the labor market very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It probably will, will place some upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That could mean that it takes longer to get to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That could mean we need to keep rates higher for longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It could even mean, ultimately, that we would need to hike again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just is—it’s the way, the way our policy works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So on, on the better-balance side, there are just a lot of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—you see—you see job growth still strong but moving back down to more sustainable levels, given population growth and labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The things that are not quite—but let me go on with that list.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, claims are low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at surveys of businesses, they’re, they’re—sort of the era of this frantic labor shortage, [those kinds of worker shortages] are behind us, and they’re seeing a shortage of labor as being significantly alleviated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at shortages of workers, whereas they thought job, job availability was the highest that it’d ever been or close to it, that’s now down to more normal levels by so many measures—participation, unemployment—so many measures: the unemployment—job openings, quits, all of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So wages are still running a bit above what would be consistent with 2 percent inflation over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’ve been gradually cooling off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if wages are running around 4 percent, that’s still a bit above, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I guess there, there are just a couple of other—the unemployment rate is very, very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And these are—but, but I would just say, overall, the development of the labor market has been very positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been a good time for workers to find jobs and get solid wage increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A common theme is that, while inflation is coming down, and that’s very good news, the price level is not coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Prices of some, some goods and services are coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But overall, in the aggregate, the price level is not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people are still living with high prices, and that’s, that’s not—that is something that people don’t like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, so what will happen with that is, wages are now—[changes in] real wages are now positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So [nominal] wages are now moving up more than inflation, as inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that might help improve the mood of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we do see those—we see those public opinion surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The thing that we can do is to do our jobs, which is to use our tools to foster price stability, which has such great benefits over such long periods of time, and which is the thing that really enables us to work for and achieve an extended period of high employment, which is so beneficial for, you know, families and, and companies around the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not something we’re hoping to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Obviously, we’re hoping to, to see something very different—which is a continuation of what we have seen, which is the labor market coming into better balance without a significant increase in unemployment, inflation coming down without a significant increase in unemployment, and growth moderating without a significant increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’re, we’re trying very much to achieve and not something that we’re looking to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, obviously, what we’ll do is we’ll look at the totality of the data, as I’ve mentioned a couple times, and, certainly, the labor data would be important in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, if you—if you can describe a situation like that where if, if there were the beginning of a recession or something like that, then, yes, that would certainly weigh heavily on that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re, we’re aware of the risk that we would hang on too long.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we know that that’s a risk, and we’re very focused on not making that mistake.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do regard the two—you know, we’ve come back into a better balance between the risk of overdoing it and the risk of underdoing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not only that, we were able to focus hard on the—on the price-stability mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re getting back to the point where—which is what you do when you’re very far from, from one of them, one of the two mandates—you’re getting now back to the point where both mandates are important, and they’re, they’re more in balance, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we’ll be—we’ll be very much keeping that in mind, as we make policy going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the things we’ll be looking at, I’ve already described.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the same thing other people see, which is a strong economy, which really put up quite a performance in 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see good evidence and good reason to believe that growth will come in lower next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you see what the forecasts are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the median growth—median participant wrote down 1.4 percent growth, but, you know, we’ll have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very hard to predict.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll also be looking to see progress on inflation and, you know, the labor market remaining strong but, but ideally, without seeing the kind of large increase in unemployment that happens sometimes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t typically tried to articulate, with one exception, really specific target levels, which was if you—some of you will remember the thresholds that we used in, I guess, 2013.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t—the answer is, these are things that we haven’t, you know, really worked out yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re sort of just at the beginning of, of that discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It wouldn’t, if that were to—first of all, let me just say, that isn’t a plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s just cumulating what people wrote down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s not something—you know this, but allow me to say it again: We don’t debate or discuss what the right, you know, whose SEP is right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just say what they are, and we tabulate them and publish them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So and it’s, you know, it’s important for people to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it wouldn’t need to be a sign of—it could just be a sign that the economy is normalizing, and it doesn’t need the tight policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So but, but it could be more of what I just described.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, that’s what we’re finding out, and we’ve, you know, we’ve seen real progress in, in core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has been sticky, and famously, the service sector is thought to be stickier, but we’ve actually seen reasonable progress in nonhousing services, which was the area where, where you would expect to see less progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are seeing some progress there, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, in fact, all three of the categories of core [prices] are now contributing: goods, housing services, nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re all contributing in different—at different levels, you know, meeting by meeting—or, rather, report by report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we got—we got CPI the morning of the first day, and we got PPI the next day, which informs the, you know, the translation into PCE [inflation].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s very late in the game, you know, to—but nonetheless, participants are allowed to, encouraged to update their SEP forecast until probably midmorning today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: After that, so staff has to—has to cumulate all of that and create the documents that you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So until about midmorning, a little, maybe late morning, it’s okay to update, and I believe some people did update their forecast based on what we saw today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The question of whether there have been fundamental structural shifts is, is really hard to know the answer and a very interesting one right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The one that would affect—the one that comes to mind, though, is just the question of where the neutral rate of interest is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, for example, if it’s risen, and I’m not saying that it has, but if it were to have risen, that would mean that, that interest rates would need to be a little bit higher to convey the same level of restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The thing is, we’re not really going to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people will be writing papers about that 10 years from now and still fighting about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s just that it’s going to be uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re going to be making policy in this, you know, difficult, uncertain, really unprecedented environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some—someone once said that you know the—you know the natural rate of interest by its works, and that’s really right, but that’s very difficult because policy operates with a lag.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s one of the reasons why we slowed down this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We started slowing down at this meeting last year, reducing the pace at which we were adding restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, over the course of this year, we really slowed down a lot to give those lags time to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s—you can make a case for that, that the shift back into services has not been complete, and it doesn’t look like it’s ongoing, but I don’t know if that’s right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Maybe people just bought so much stuff that they temporarily don’t want any more stuff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They haven’t got anyplace to put it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] MICHELLE SMITH.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let’s go to Jennifer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, the reason you wouldn’t wait to get to 2 percent to cut rates is that policy would be, it would be too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, you’d want to be reducing restriction on the economy well before 2 percent because—or before you get to 2 percent so you don’t overshoot, if we think, think of restrictive policy as weighing on economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it takes—it takes a while for policy to get into the economy, affect economic activity, and affect inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I can’t give you a precise answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you look at what’s in the—in the SEP, and, you know, I think you’ll see a reasonable estimate of the time lags and things like that that it would take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t want to—I wouldn’t want to identify any one precise point, because I would be able to look back then and probably find out that it turned out not to be right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’ll be looking at it and, and looking at the broad collection of factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think—I think this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we felt since the beginning that it would be a combination of two factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The first factor is just the unwinding of, of what happened in the pandemic: the distortions of supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the second thing would be our policy, which was weighing on aggregate demand and actually making it easier for the supply side to recover because of lower demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We thought those two things were going to be necessary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sorry, say your—say the last part of your question again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not that—it may or may not be about “different,” the U.S. economy being different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that this inflation was not the classic demand overload, pot-boiling-over, kind of inflation that we [typically] think about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was a combination of very strong demand, without question, and unusual supply-side restrictions, both on the goods side but also on the labor side, because we had a—we had a participation shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is just very unusual.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we had the view—my colleagues and I broadly had the view—that we could get a lot of—you know, you had essentially a vertical supply curve, because you ran into the limits of, of capacity at very low levels, because there weren’t workers and because people couldn’t—the supply chains were all broken.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we had the view that you could come straight down that vertical supply curve to the extent demand [was] lowered, reduced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, something like that has happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It happened so far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It might.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Immigration could help, but it may be that, at some point—at some point, you will run out of supply-side help, and then it gets down to demand, and it gets harder.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s very possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But to say with certainty that the last mile is going to be different, I’d be reluctant to, you know, to suggest that we have any certainty around that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, inflation keeps coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market keeps getting back into balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s so far, so good—although we kind of assume that it will get harder from here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But so far, it hasn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, we’re not talking about altering the pace of QT right now, just to get that out of the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the balance sheet seems to be working pretty much as expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we’ve been seeing is, you know, that we’re allowing runoff each month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s adding up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’re down—we’re close to 1.2 trillion [dollars].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s showing up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The reverse repo facility [take-up] has been coming down quickly, and reserves have been either moving up or—as a result—or holding steady.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At a certain point, you know, there won’t be any more to come out of, or there’ll be a level where [take-up at] the reverse repo facility levels out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, at that point, reserves will start to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we still have—you know that we intend to reduce our securities holdings until we judge that the quantity of reserve balances has reached a level somewhat above that consistent with ample reserves, and we also intend to slow and then stop the decline in size of the balance sheet when reserve balances are somewhat above the level judged to be consistent with ample reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not at those levels, you know, with, with reserves close to 3.5 trillion [dollars].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not—we don’t think we’re at those [levels judged consistent with ample] reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There isn’t a lot of evidence of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re watching it carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, so far—so far, it’s working pretty much as expected, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think they’re, they’re on independent tracks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the answer is, it depends on the reason.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, if you’re—if you’re—if you’re cutting rates because you’re going back to normal, that’s one thing, [and distinct from] if you’re cutting them because the economy is really weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you can imagine, you’d have to know what the reason is to know whether it would be appropriate to do those two things at the same time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks very much.
